en: The Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds, Scroll One; also titled *The Laudatory Biography of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Baoyun of Liangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Causes and Conditions. Chapter One: On Causes and Conditions.
Now I have roughly proclaimed the Dharma; listen with a compassionate mind and receive it.
These essential meanings of the Buddha’s many sutras are the words of the Holy Teacher.
These scriptures transmitted from the Buddha are of the greatest benefit to the world.
The recipient receives great celebration, and their moisture benefits all living beings.
Among all Buddhas, sages, and the wisdom of the vidyārājas,
those who invoke the name with a compassionate heart shall obtain immeasurable merit.
I now therefore expound this auspiciousness, whereby sorrow and suffering are forever extinguished;
in whatever region one goes, there shall be no lack of peace and security.
Examine your feelings and single-mindedly guard your hearts; each of you listen with a tranquil mind.
Those who uphold this teaching shall cleanse away all defilements.
With the pure water of the Dharma, they diligently wash their minds;
entering the deep pool of nirvana, their physical form becomes exceedingly radiant.
The five desires are like galloping horses; the whole world follows them into delusion.
Whirling about without a way out, they are deceived and led astray by wearying cravings.
Some race through blinding darkness, wandering alone through the five realms of existence.
With the bridle of wisdom, skillfully guide and turn back the deluded mind;
with the whip of impermanence, strike and restrain the horse of sensual desire;
break the spirit of greed, and cause the will to abandon flattery.
The rivers of the six realms of desire flow on; the rush toward evil is exceedingly swift.
One should employ the power of wisdom to construct firm and thick embankments and dikes.
Delighting in the toil and suffering of birth and death, one never finds rest.
With a mind of insatiable craving, one is intoxicated by the five desires.
The eight kinds of medicinal decoctions, blended with great divine efficacy;
by partaking of their nectar-like flavor in accordance with the teaching, one who was intoxicated shall soon awaken.
The various classes of beings within the three realms, their hands pointed by perverted views,
are inverted within the five destinies like bouncing balls.
On the verge of escaping to the end of suffering, they fall back again into birth and death.
Now that I have heard the holy and luminous teaching, I should extinguish my deluded mind.
The radiance of compassion shines universally upon the world;
yet the fool perceives it as a mirage in the heat, his ignorant heart naturally bewildered.
Birth and death are like a vast marsh, where a solitary fawn becomes lost;
one should drink the milk of the Dharma to eliminate long-standing hunger and thirst.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been sucked dry by old age and death.
One does not rejoice at seeing good medicine, but instead reviles and slanders the physician.
The physician has prepared thirty-seven kinds of mixed medicinal divine ointments;
one should seek them through skillful means and diligently take them to eliminate the affliction.
In the long night of worldly afflictions, sentient beings sleep soundly;
you should prepare the drum of ambrosia to awaken them so they do not remain in slumber.
The Buddha-sun has appeared in the world, illuminating the bountiful autumn of the Dharma.
One should, with the eye of wisdom, diligently and universally observe:
the minds of sentient beings are like water—restless, turbid, and lacking clarity;
by settling them with the Dharma, they become clear, just like the waters in autumn.
Sentient beings who skillfully govern their minds, with concentrated thoughts free from agitation and turbidity,
will swiftly find their destination and enter the ocean of Nirvana.
Though they manifest various transformed bodies throughout the long duration of birth and death, [they remain steadfast].
Devas, humans, and the three evil realms— hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—
should now abandon their treacherous deceptions and their forms of flattery, falsehood, and hypocrisy;
entering the city of extinguished lapis lazuli, they shall become one single color.
There was a king named Aśoka, who brought peace and prosperity to his realm;
he caused his enemies to dwell in sorrow and fear, while those who submitted to him were filled with joy and reverence.
Throughout this entire land, he erected eighty-four thousand stūpas.
The devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits rejoice, and their voices shake the world.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi spirits hear this thundering sound;
as the Buddha-dharma becomes even more flourishing and radiant, they consequently turn their minds to recollect the Buddha.
With head bowed and cheek resting on his hand, he sat in dejection.
Only when the Buddha was in the world did the various devas ask him:
"O Benevolent One, why do you grieve?"
Gazing intently for a long while, he then let out a deep sigh;
with a voice trembling with grief and despondency, he spoke these words in reply:
"The Buddha, the Teacher among gods and men, has bestowed the sublime teaching upon devas and humans."
"Because I recall the Buddha, the Holy Honored One, I am thus filled with sorrow and distress!
These various devas and humans were later reborn and did not see the Buddha;
only after the Buddha had passed into extinction were they born in the heavens.
Upon first hearing the name of the Buddha, the hairs on my body all stood erect;
with a heart of loving respect, I then questioned the Vajra deity:
"O Benevolent One, who is this Buddha?"
What virtuous and sublime qualities do you possess?
What power of wisdom do you possess?
What laws of discipline and restraint do you possess?
What is his appearance like?
With what does he adorn himself?
We pray that you, O Benevolent One, will deign to look upon us and explain this in detail for our sake.
With these words of radiant light, he exhorted the Vajra deity;
speaking like a flower in full bloom, with a smile and a serene countenance, he said:
"The profound and subtle Dharma you inquire about is difficult to explain in haste."
The various sages cannot fathom it; how could I alone possibly describe it?
If one could use a finger to lift up the earth of the world-system, and if one could inhale all the deep pools and oceans of the four seas until they were entirely exhausted—
If one could entirely swallow up the Iron Ring Mountains and the Diamond Mountains;
if one could bind and suspend Mount Sumeru with the fibers of a lotus root;
and if one wished to encircle and wrap it until the very limits of empty space were exhausted—
If one further wishes to calculate and know the number of sentient beings in the ten directions, this matter is still easily achieved; by studying it, one might perhaps succeed.
But if one wishes to extol the Buddha’s merits, no one is able to do so exhaustively.
May I rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, so that my mind may not err;
may I be able to proclaim even a little, praising the Buddha’s virtuous qualities.
What I now speak is like the speech of a parrot.
"Out of joy for you, O virtuous ones, you should listen with single-minded attention.
**Chapter Two: Praising the Tathāgata** *From the Buddhacarita Sūtra* Now I wish to ascend to the pure void, To soar through the Buddha’s peerless Dharma;
Yet as I am about to utter these words, My heart is filled with deep hesitation.
The feathers and wings of my mind are weak in power and cannot be made strong;
the Buddha’s wisdom of emptiness and non-existence encompasses everything beyond the vast void.
Even if there were a man of great strength who exerted all his might to shoot at the empty sky, [he could not reach it].
An arrow may travel through kalpas, yet it cannot reach the limit of space; so too,
though the various sages and saints possess brilliant wisdom,
they cannot exhaustively praise the Buddha’s virtue through their immeasurable eloquence regarding the Buddha’s great wisdom of emptiness.
Having already crossed to the shore beyond suffering, you have dried up the river of craving and desire;
you have blocked the abyss of birth, old age, and death, and opened the way for the great ocean of Dharma.
Neither gods nor humans, nor those of heterodox arts, can exhaust the source of your intent.
Therefore, the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom is profound, without shore or bottom.
Just as the various heavens dwell atop Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, the Buddha’s virtues are like Sumeru; none can see its summit.
The Demon King advanced his three daughters, coming to disturb the resolve of the Way;
wherever they went, none failed to be deluded, yet only the Buddha’s compassion could protect him.
Eighteen billion demon kings transformed their appearances and came seeking battle;
The Buddha extends his arm from his robe, Like the sun shining red through the clouds.
With hands marked by a hundred blessings, He points toward the earth to subdue the Māra King;
Dare not to face the Buddha’s virtue, Like gazing at the sunlight in the darkness.
The gods are unable to destroy the haughty banner of Māra;
only the Buddha can shatter it, for the Buddha has raised the great banner of the Dharma.
As for the other kings of affliction, who possess powerful strength and harbor malice and harm—
The Māra of Delusion and the Māra of Death lead their armies and progeny;
Craving gives birth to the sons of the five hindrances, who first scale the heights to shroud and envelop the world.
Others advance with intent to harm, manifesting in various forms.
Anger, malice, haste, stinginess, and envy; The feverish affliction of pride and arrogance;
Perverse views and craving within the realm of desire— These are the kings of false delusion and worldly toil.
Their harmful intent is powerful and oppressive; They surround one, seeking to engage in battle.
They bind together the battle array of afflictions, each displaying the strength of their martial equipment.
Each discharges fierce and powerful bows to strike the ordinary and ignorant;
those arrows are like venomous snakes and are also like blazing fires.
Since the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there has been no one to oppose him;
though the Buddha’s virtues shielded his arrows, they only caused the burning embers to flare up even more intensely.
He mounts the chariot of the merit of precepts and dons the sturdy armor of patience.
Mounted upon the steed of diligence, he enters the battle against the dust of afflictions.
With the sharp spearhead of right view, with right intention as his arrow;
with right speech as its feathers, and right action as its nock.
Taking the Right Path as the arrowhead, Drawing it from within the tube of the mind;
Releasing the bow of compassion with swift dispatch— The Buddha’s arrows are named the Four Immeasurables.
A single discharge extinguishes the afflictions, Shaking the trichiliocosm.
Wisdom burns away the dust of desire, Just as an army is consumed by fire.
Generosity, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, Wisdom, faith, and steadfastness;
Guarding one’s resolve without wavering, Is like the many rivers flowing into the sea.
The world is luminous within the void; throughout the ten directions, all receive peace.
With a mind fixed and firm, one contemplates the arising and ceasing of the world.
Having attained the adamantine mind, one shatters the mountain of worldly toil.
Beholding with the Buddha-eye, the three thousandfold world-system is like a mirror.
The various immortals of external studies have long practiced yet attained no realization;
the One of All-Knowledge has no teacher, and is thus named the Teacher of Teachers.
With the adamantine beak of powerful wisdom, he shatters the solid egg of ignorance;
Escaping the prison of delusion and darkness, he soars above the unconditioned and pure void.
In the heavens, he partakes of ambrosia; on earth, he eats the *sālī* rice or the horse-herd’s barley.
He took no pleasure in celestial flavors, nor did he suffer from the horse-herder’s grain.
When Devadatta raged and hurled a stone, Rāhula stood before him;
both gazed with eyes of compassion, seeing poison and sandalwood as equal.
Though reviled by those of external paths, he is praised by devas and humans;
unmoved in either circumstance, he is like trying to blow away Mount Sumeru with one's breath.
His fame resounds through the three thousandfold world-system; the Buddha is the Teacher of the entire universe.
Though slandered by those with evil intent, his mind remains equanimous, free from joy or grief. Whether facing folly,
gain, loss, defamation, praise, renown, censure, suffering, or pleasure—
these eight worldly conditions cannot stain him, just as a lotus flower remains untainted by water.
The pleasures of heavens and the human world are viewed by him as all unreal;
he regards the world as a foolish game, seeing that all that has form is empty and non-existent.
For the sentient beings of the three evil realms, he opens the gate that is so difficult to open.
He empties the three evil realms and hells, leading devas and humans to the unconditioned.
He traverses the paths and delivers those of the three periods; he binds the *asuras* and their arrogance.
He exhorts the multitude toward the roots of goodness and rains down the Three Jewels upon the world.
In ages past, the Wheel-Turning Kings exercised sovereignty over the four quarters;
yet even they could not follow their own will, for they escaped death only to reach the Unconditioned.
The Buddha cultivated various karmas to govern the empty city of the Dharma.
Delivering beings from the thieves of worldly toil, he leads them toward the city of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
The sun’s brilliance illuminates the day but not the night, nor does it shine upon the three evil realms in the heavens;
the Buddha’s light shines through day and night across the three thousandfold world-system, reaching even into the minds of all sentient beings.
The Buddha’s wondrous radiance is ever brilliant and vast, beyond comparison with tens of millions of countless lights;
like the full moon on the fifteenth day, its brilliance illuminates the night but adds nothing to the day.
The Lord of Devas was filled with grief and distress as his life drew to its end;
on the verge of falling away and losing his celestial merit, he approached the Buddha and again realized the Truth.
The Sun and Moon, the eyes of the world, were being harassed by the Asuras.
The Buddha’s compassion rescues the world, saving it so that it does not encounter calamity.
The smoke of anxiety is like a flickering flame; the desire for pleasure is like taking medicine;
attachment is likened to a raging fire, which the Buddha extinguishes with the water of the Dharma.
Harboring resentment and extreme rage, intent on harm;
intoxicated by drink, crazed and deluded—Aṅgulimāla and the rutting elephant were subdued by the Buddha through his compassion.
Bound tightly by the firm fetters of immeasurable births and deaths, the thief of ignorance blinds their eyes.
The Buddha used the medicine of wisdom to plug his speech, decisively eliminating the thieves of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
These three men possessed such thick layers of defilement that even if śrāvakas were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, none could move a single hair on them;
only the Buddha could rescue them and cause them to behold the light of the Way.
His appearance was exceedingly haughty, due to his robes of precious brocade;
yet the most arrogant among the scattered sands, upon seeing the Buddha, bowed and performed prostrations.
His head seemed to wear a crown of flames, his tusks were long, and his eyes were a deep crimson.
When enraged, he hurls fire to burn; yet the Buddha subdues the Āḷavaka demon.
When the Dragon King harbors poisonous wrath, his hail destroys the kingdom of Magadha;
the Buddha shakes the earth and causes mountains to crumble, his majestic power extinguishing the dragon’s venom.
The Buddha is like a great elephant king, Entering the lotus pond of birth-and-death;
Treading upon the weeds of worldly toil, He stands poised within nirvāṇa.
The Buddha guides beings across birth-and-death, Like an ox crossing a flowing river.
Sentient beings have crossed over until now, like a herd of oxen following a guide.
The Buddha is like a pool of the eight liberations, where the Dharma gives rise to lotus flowers;
devas and humans are like bees gathering there, and by partaking of the fragrance, they leave suffering behind.
The devas heard that at the bottom of the ocean there was the medicine of immortality;
because the great Nāga King of the ocean entwined Mount Sumeru,
the devas and asuras pulled at the sea for a thousand years.
Employing various skillful means, he exerted himself with great diligence and hardship;
drawing forth the essence of ten thousand kinds of medicinal herbs, he caused them to coalesce upon the water.
Believing this to be the medicine of immortality, he took it up and placed it in a golden vessel.
Those who wear these garments do not attain eternal life; they cannot escape old age, sickness, and death.
Yet, with a mind free from delusion, one holds the divine medicine and turns the wheel without end.
The Buddha, by means of the seven factors of enlightenment, uses the power of wisdom to grasp the great ocean.
Encompassed by the meditative absorption of cessation, Drawn forth by the power of diligence,
It brings forth the ambrosial medicine, Permanently extinguishing old age and illness;
The supreme bliss that extinguishes all suffering— Whoever partakes of it leaves birth and death behind.
The Buddha’s brilliance is like the sun, its essence undisturbed; his fullness is like the moon at its peak, yet without cold.
His bliss surpasses that of the six heavens while he eliminates desire; his radiance is like a blazing fire that leaves nothing unburnt.
The Dharma is most subtle and profound, its virtuous conduct complete; it is a treasury of all goodness, praised as a mass of merit.
It universally gathers the excellence of gods and humans; one never tires of admiring and praising the Buddha’s virtues.
Radiant as the sun and bright as the moon, pleasing to the eye like a flower and thundering with a voice like a roll of drums;
walking like a king of elephants and patient as the earth—the Buddha alone is supreme, surpassing all in the world.
Such immeasurable, pure, and wondrous praises, though all the sages were to exhaust an eon, could not fully describe them;
how much less can I, in my ignorance and shallowness, hope to reach their end? It would be like attempting to cross the ocean without a boat.
All the devas joined their palms in reverence, Their hearts filled with joy, they called him Vajra;
They prayed that the Buddha would descend from Tuṣita, And he immediately granted his consent to preach for them.
Chapter 3: Descent into the Womb From the *Buddhacarita*, Chapter Three: Descent into the Womb. While dwelling in the Tuṣita palace, He surveyed everywhere with his divine eye.
Beholding the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, I recall my vows from antiquity.
My original vow was to bring peace to all beings; through successive kalpas, I have labored in the quest for Buddhahood.
Though life after life I encountered hardships, I never grew weary of planting the roots of virtue.
This is the foremost of supreme offerings: from the time he first resolved upon his aspiration, he has bestowed gold everywhere;
through the virtue of his generous giving, his hands have become perfected.
From these various acts of giving at the very beginning, those who hear of them find their hair standing on end.
Head, eyes, body, hands, and feet; wife and children, those held most dear;
grand carriages with famous elephants and horses;
jeweled chariots draped with pearls—if all these were gathered together, the entire earth would not be able to contain them.
The thunderous roar of his diligent giving is like the descent of celestial rain;
through the waters of wisdom across kalpas, he universally moistens and satisfies all sentient beings.
He bestows pools of curd and rivers of milk; his mountain of merit has ghee flowing like a spring.
Moat-filled with honey, piled high with refined sugar, universally adorning this ground;
never failing those who seek, giving with no resistance;
pouring water into the hands of recipients, comparable to the four great oceans.
Serving one's parents and enlightened teachers with a compassionate heart and all manner of services;
bestowing gifts without limit or end—this accomplishes the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā).
In every life one maintains superior precepts, never defiling the prohibitions even unto death.
Shaving one's head to become a śramaṇa, though the hair thus shorn could be piled up like a great mountain,
one gives rise to the five desires of the foolish; yet, encountering life-threatening dangers,
one remains unmoved and does not violate the pure precepts— this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Born with noble freedom, he never inflicted harm upon others;
even when his head, eyes, hands, and feet were severed, his mind remained steadfast in patience.
With a heart awakened to the truth, he resolved to seek Buddhahood, attaining progress that transcended nine kalpas.
Maitreya and others should go first; let the valiant ones precede them.
Out of longing for the profound and wondrous Dharma, they shall receive the meaning of wisdom through their bodies;
they will enter fire, throw themselves from mountain cliffs, and have their limbs pinned with iron needles.
The wisdom of the eighteen dharmas is practiced without the arising of weariness;
awakening to the origin of all things, one crosses to the shore of infinite knowledge.
Generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, and concentration are the deep pools of the ocean of wisdom.
Compassion for suffering beings brings about the radiance of joy.
From his pores, light of various colors shines forth, illuminating and shaking the Tuṣita Palace.
The devas, gathering with doubts in their hearts, pay reverent homage to the Bodhisattva.
Immediately, various golden drums were struck, And provisions were bestowed as stakes for the seven factors of enlightenment;
"Who wishes to descend into the world with me?
Therefore, I extend this invitation to the assembly of Dharma guests."
Light radiated from Tuṣita, illuminating the four quarters; delighting in service and labor, it reached Jambudvīpa.
He then commanded his attendant minister, the noble Yue Meng:
"You know the great kings of the world."
"In what land may I take rebirth?
Without contravening the ancient traditions,
I shall encounter a Bodhisattva and reverently follow the Buddha’s teachings."
He replied:
"May the Holy One listen: There is a great and noble king; there is a king named Suprabha who rules over the city of Rājagṛha."
The lord of the city of Vārāṇasī was a king named Sumati;
the king of Śakya was Śata-kauśalya; the king of Udyāna was named Nara;
the king of Arciṣmat was Roca; and there was also a king named Śūra-vikrama.
The son of King Subāhu is also known as King Śvetaketu.
These eight great kings are renowned; I wonder whether it would be appropriate for [the Bodhisattva] to take birth among them?
He said: "There is this king’s impurity and lack of truth; let us examine thoroughly that which is true.
After reflecting for a moment, he said:

"There is yet another: after the lineage of the Cakravartin kings has flourished for a long time, there will be a king named Siṃha at the height of his prosperity; his son shall be Śuddhodana, the Honored One among the Śākyas."
“Excellent and wondrous, he accords with my heart’s desire; he should be entrusted to be born as my son.
Śuddhodana is the foremost among men, and Māyā is the most eminent among women.
Among all cities and towns, Kapilavastu is the best.”
Today I shall descend, bestowing goodness upon the world;
showing the right path to sentient beings, I shall shatter the shackles and fetters of desire.
I will destroy the prison of birth and death, and reveal the path to the unconditioned.
I manifest skillful means for sentient beings, to cause them to emerge from the prison of birth and death.
Among you all, who desires to leave suffering behind and attain the peace of nirvana?
Those who wish to deliver themselves from suffering, descend with me.
Having proclaimed this Dharma, he descended from the Tuṣita palace;
manifesting the vehicle so that all may know it, the white elephant was like a mountain of silver.
The Bodhisattva, riding upon the king of elephants, was like the sun shining upon white clouds.
The devas played drums and danced, raining down flowers of various colors everywhere.
The sun-essence mani-jewel shone brilliantly within the royal palace;
as he descended from the divine realm to take birth, most subtle and wondrous omens appeared.
The Bodhisattva descends into the womb like a swan in a clear pool;
like the full autumn moon’s radiance, like an elephant in a flower pond.
As the sun shines with its light, as the moon displays its brilliant pearls.
The Bodhisattva is beyond all comparison; he dwells only with virtue and merit.
Once he was in the womb of the sublime queen, the earth shook in six ways;
it was like a boat upon the water, or the crashing roar of thunder in the sky.
The ocean pools stir with solemnity, and the myriad streams become pure and clear;
the devas in the sky spread flowers like canopies.
Uttering cries of celebration, they leap for joy; the earth spirits smile with delight.
All the flowers have fully blossomed in fresh splendor, covering the ground without any gaps.
When the tree-spirit beholds the many flowers, she opens wide like eyes gazing upon them;
but Māra, who loves this tree, immediately withers and grows haggard with grief.
The Sublime Queen, having awakened from her sleep, immediately recalled her dream; her faculties were serene as she leaped for joy.
Raising her eyes and looking in all four directions, she beheld the King’s countenance, as pleasant and radiant as a lotus flower.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"Please listen; what was seen in my dream is most auspicious.
A great white elephant king with six tusks suddenly arrived before me."
When the king heard of the queen’s dream, he was filled with both doubt and exultation;
he immediately summoned a brahmin diviner and recounted what he had seen in his dream.
The diviner, who was wise and skilled in interpreting dreams, reflected deeply before speaking.
According to the classics on the interpretation of dreams, listen now to this true explanation:
"The woman’s dream of the sun’s radiance entering her womb indicates that she shall conceive and give birth to an auspicious son;
like the sun shining brilliantly upon the entire world, his virtue shall be honored and he shall rule the ten directions."
In a dream he saw the full moon together with all sentient beings; Its light shone upon the woman’s womb, by which she conceived.
She gave birth to a sage who turned the golden wheel, Ruling over the four quarters through the administration of the True Dharma.
"This woman dreamed of a white elephant entering her right flank;
this son is free from all blemish, and gods and humans bow their heads in homage.
There is nothing he does not know; he who is born shall surely become a Buddha."
This scripture is an ancient sage’s prophecy: the Queen dreamed of a white elephant;
she shall give birth to a precious and holy son, a divine sage who walks with the solitary stride of an elephant.
By divining with the hexagram An (Peace), it is certain that he will be born as a Teacher of Gods and Humans.

"There are only two destinies for him: either he will rule as a holy king within the household, or he will renounce the home, shave his hair and beard, and become a Buddha, a teacher of the multitude of sages.
Delighted by the truth of this dream interpretation, he bestowed gold upon him to his heart's content.
When the queen heard this, she was greatly delighted and informed the king of these auspicious matters:
"Since I had this dream, it has been as sweet as drinking nectar;
all my inherent evils have been removed, and I now desire only to delight in all that is good."
One does not delight in robes of precious jewels, but only in pure, simple, and clean garments;
one does not favor fans made of precious gems, but delights in the cool breeze of the open air.
One feels revulsion for the five desires and takes pleasure in receiving the true and correct Dharma.
"The six sense-faculties no longer cling to forms, sounds, scents, tastes, or tangibles;
one no longer delights in palaces, as the mind roams through gardens and pavilions.
Having addressed the king in this way, the king immediately replied:
"Following your pleasure, O King, let us depart together;
even the displaced people shall go to the Cool Grove of Flowering Trees.
The Queen, observing her own body within, saw it as like the reflection of the moon in clear water."
Remaining in the womb without defilement, borne in a carriage of golden flowers and lapis lazuli;
with the months complete and all faculties perfected, he appeared like a precious, luminous pearl.
When the Queen perceived that the time for his birth had arrived, she went to stroll in the Garden of Fragrant Flowers.
That garden was solemn and pure, where various wondrous deities gathered.
Chapter Four: The Birth of the Tathāgata, from the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds*. At that time, the constellation Puṣya coincided with the moon;
auspicious signs appeared in accordance with the season, and he was born from the right side [of his mother].
Just as when the clouds are cleared away, the thousand suns suddenly appear;
or like a long-standing darkness, where the light of a torch suddenly shines forth.
The trees are her hair, the flowering grasses are her body hair, and the lotus flowers are her face.
The blue lotus is her eyes; the vermilion trees are her mouth; Mount Sumeru is her breasts; the four seas are her belly;
the Central Land is her waist; the Southern Continent is her hips;
Pūrvavideha is her pendant pearl; the Ganges is her fragrant necklace; and Aparagoyānī is her feet.
Adorned with various jewels,
these were the successive sovereigns of the universal wheel-turning kings;
as numerous as the sands of rivers, they were all trodden upon by the Buddha.
With the thousand-spoked wheel-mark, his vehicle is ever-yoked;
it is the virtue and righteousness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past.
He nurtures and gives birth to all things, just like a compassionate mother.
At that moment of being difficult to move, a solemn and trembling sound arose.
With hearts full of joy and composed dignity, they gazed with harmonious delight;
at that very instant, from his right side, there appeared a great and brilliant radiance.
He obstructs the light of the sun, making the sun appear like a firefly;
he causes the sun to lose its sight, so that it no longer possesses its brilliant radiance.
Its light is like a flowered topknot, manifesting manifold colors.
Filling the four quarters and pervading the void of space,
it was as if clouds had been cleared away and the sun suddenly appeared;
at that time, the various devas beheld the brilliant, radiant light.
Trembling with awe and struck by the marvel, they said to one another:
"Is the sun falling from the heavens?
Has a golden tree emerged?"
A deity replied,
"The Buddha-sun has appeared.
The Sun Deity wondered, "What kind of extraordinary sun is this?"
"Lest he should deprive me [of my merit]," thought the Sun; yet his jealousy vanished instantly as he beheld those thousand rays of light.
The Buddha’s radiance illuminates the earth; the sun’s flames shine upon the sky.
The Prince harbors a light a thousand times greater than the sun;
the sunlight turns back and retreats, unable to face it.
Heaven and earth were universally ablaze, like the flames at the end of an eon;
heaven and earth were bright and opened wide, like the dawn of the beginning of time.
All the gods were filled with universal joy, and the terrestrial deities danced with exultation.
Rays of light shower down like rain, a sublime medicine of ambrosia;

as I observe now, his mind’s discernment is such that how could his practice and training ever accord with yours?
With a face like the full moon and a tongue like a flower petal,
he shall surely drink dry the entire ocean of wisdom.
Beholding the Bodhisattva’s gait, it is as if the Moon Deva has descended.
Thereupon all the brahmins sighed that it was unprecedented;
their hearts were filled with leaping joy, like the surging waves of the deep ocean.
Within their minds they felt great delight, as if the moonlight had appeared in the midst of darkness.
The Prince, seeing these various [ascetics], each practicing their own particular disciplines and displaying all manner of emaciated forms, was moved with sorrow and sighed in lamentation:
"How extreme is this evil! How they are deluded by ignorance!"
"The world is pitiable and tragic; Deluded in their conduct, they forcibly enter suffering.
With a mind free of self, like a great elephant king, Trembling with fear, he emerges from the forest of blazing fires.
The golden radiance shines brilliantly upon the forest trees;
It is like the autumn sun passing through the blue clouds.
Beholding the constant flow of the myriad streams As they reach the ocean, the king of waters;
With flocks of wild geese and white cranes, he fashioned white pearl necklaces;
using the surging currents of the great flood, he made them into precious bracelets and armlets;
arriving at the banks of the Ganges, he was like the King of the Sea Spirits himself.
Adorned throughout his body with the marks of a hundred merits,
he entered the waters of the Ganges, whereby all its currents became clear and pure.
The deities dwelling within all the waters rose from below to receive his feet.
In a brief moment he had passed through [the city], like a king of geese.
Having then crossed the Ganges River, knowing it was time to act according to the season,
he cast away all prideful thoughts and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Clad in the robes of a śramaṇa, wearing a saffron-colored *kāṣāya*,
he had stilled his faculties through meditative concentration and moved with perfect dignity.
Beholding the Prince’s physical marks, his merit shone forth most majestically.
He wears the robe of tranquil extinction, its color corresponding to pure conduct.
All the people are struck with amazement; though agitated, they harbor joy.
Gazing intently at the Bodhisattva’s form, their eyes remain fixed upon him as if bound.
The assembly gazed upon this bodhisattva, their minds never weary;
His merit from past lives is complete, and all his marks are fully possessed.
He is like a wondrous lotus flower, with stalks of a thousand varieties of colors.
The multitude went to behold him, like bees gathering at a lotus flower;
wherever he turned his course, the multitude followed him all together,
just as the various faculties of a person follow the mind as it wanders about.
As they conversed with one another in succession, they marveled at his merit;
observing this man, they saw he was a sublime jewel among men.
They gazed intently upon his eyes and the wondrous beauty of his countenance.
It is like a heap of gold dust, within which lies a kingly sapphire;
encircled by radiance, it is formed by the accumulation of virtuous marks;
its appearance is most harmonious, and all the secondary signs are fully complete.
Filling the minds of all people, their eyes follow him together;
gazing upon him repeatedly and with keen attention, they never grow weary of it.
It is as if encountering a heavy snowstorm, where the cold and freezing are most intense and piercing.
The multitude vied with one another to move forward, as if they had obtained fire in a cauldron of boiling water.
Women of noble lineage each rushed out from their houses,
like flashes of brilliant lightning emerging from thick clouds.
Just as the aśoka tree, with its branches, leaves, and flowers in full bloom,
bends and inclines when struck by the wind, so do they pay homage to the Bodhisattva.
Cradling infants upon their laps, they all let the milk flow from their breasts.
Gazing intently at the Bodhisattva, they forgot to return for the milk.
All the people within the city joined together in competition to praise him;
each said, "This is excellent," "This is marvelous," "This is a wondrous sign."
At that time, one person said:
"If someone were suddenly to ask, 'Is this stone-melting cake sweet or is it not?
and if one were to praise only one aspect of its appearance; [how could one fully describe it?]"
"One cannot speak of them as merely one, for they are a vast accumulation of manifold virtues.
Through the discerning consciousness of ultimate truth, all manner of goodness is fully revealed;
it adorns the body and fills the hearts and eyes of men.
Adorned with various flowers upon her countenance, And moved by the fragrance of soft incense,
she is like the springtime of the sun, Radiant and brilliantly shining.
Since this is the retribution for past deeds, How could she lack a heart of compassion?
Because he begs with this celestial form, he does not act as a sovereign king over the entire earth.
Consciousness is able to recognize this: that his practice consists of begging from others;
who could possibly give to such a person? There is no one to be found who would do so.
At that time, the king, whose name was Bimbisāra,
was atop a high pavilion; seeing from afar the Prince walking,
he immediately asked his attendants:
"Who is this practitioner?
His appearance is most radiant, yet he wears robes of plain color.
A courtier immediately addressed the king, extensively recounting his lineage and caste.
The King commanded his attendants, saying:
"Observe where he goes.
Having finished eating outside the city, he placed his bowl upon a mountain peak.
The light and shadows shone brilliantly, like the sun rising over a mountain ridge.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, accompanied only by his retinue, arrived at Mount Paṇḍava; his attire and appearance were extraordinary.
Attendants held precious parasols as he moved with the graceful, auspicious gait of a lion;
the King descended from his jeweled chariot and ascended the mountain step by step.
There he saw the Prince sitting alone, his faculties stilled and extinguished.
Like the full moon suddenly appearing above the clouds,
or like the forms and images of all phenomena manifesting in an instant;
his mind was filled with great astonishment, and looking toward his ministers, he said:
"Those who possess such physical form and features, whose appearance is lovely and pleasing;
these can surely be relied upon now, for they are capable of achieving great and virtuous merit.
Now, observing their manifold virtues, they are supple and gentle."
Briefly observing its essential features, he thought, "Only a Buddha could possess such a mark.
Setting aside his prideful thoughts and maintaining humility,
the king, according to the propriety of the occasion, greeted the Bodhisattva with inquiries of well-being.
With a pure mind, the king sat down before him upon a green stone;
he then addressed the Bodhisattva and, for this reason, spoke these verses:
“The ancestral lineage of the Prince originates from the Sun Deity.”
Though my years are still in the prime of youth, my physical form is exceedingly radiant.
Not knowing the cause of this, I have given rise to this thought:
to sustain myself by begging, rather than relishing the worldly throne of a king.
His graceful appearance is most serene and radiant; having accumulated merit, he is naturally joyful.
He is like a jambu tree, with its many flowers in full and glorious bloom.
Clad in this *kāṣāya*, it is as if he were wrapped in grass.
Like tree blossoms fearing the snow, they dare not display their brilliance.
Your Highness ought to wear the famous jewels of the heavens;
these plain-colored robes are by no means suitable for you.
If there were a pure object, yet even a slight impurity could be censured;
though it is manifest and fully apparent, there is no means by which it can be removed.
His arms are exceedingly long and beautiful, like pillars of purple-gold.
It is fitting to adorn it with the seven treasures and to wield a wondrous bow;
such an arm as this should only be used for giving in charity.
It is not fitting to use this hand to beg from others.
If you persist in your humility and refuse to accept the position of your father;
now I, with all my love and respect, entreat you to visit our humble kingdom.
Enjoy all the honors and emoluments we possess within this kingdom of Magadha.
If you wish to govern the lands everywhere, I, your humble servant, shall personally assist you.
With a countenance such as yours, endowed with the virtue of benevolence, you ought to encompass both heaven and the world;
yet, if you merely hold them in your hand, how could the governance of heaven and the world be a labor to you?
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, arose from among them to become a minister;
how much more so for those like us, the kings upon this earth.
I do not grow weary of wholesome dharmas, nor do I find distress in upholding righteousness.
It is not the time to abandon the life of renunciation; this alone is what troubles my mind.
At first, one is like a youth in the prime of life, but once that has passed, the will grows weak.
When the faculties have been disciplined and well-tamed, they are as easy to turn back as a horse with its bridle.
Generosity, wisdom, and self-restraint through the precepts are the very face of all practices;
they reveal the deeds of former lives and lead one to encounter past roots of goodness.
As the years pass and one grows older, it is only then that one can truly uphold the Dharma.
Though advanced in years, my mind remains disciplined; I do not pursue various sensual desires.
For this reason, it is not possible for my physical form to be exhausted;
now that I have attained this auspicious blessing, I may enjoy food in accordance with the Dharma.
The desirable objects of the six senses are like a response that fills and increases;
only then does one go forth to seek the nectar-like Dharma of liberation.
The radiance of his countenance surpasses the brilliance of the sun.
His benevolent virtue has already transcended and surpassed all those in the world, both gods and humans.
Such a thing has never been heard of since antiquity, nor has it ever been seen;
at such a form and appearance, all who behold him are struck with amazement.
Now, beholding the Crown Prince’s deportment and graceful bearing,
and observing the foundation of his resolve, it is exceedingly fierce, sharp, and firm—
like the depths of a deep abyss where schools of fish swim about.
Although it does not manifest above, its external movement can be discerned.
Now, observing the various patterns, they are hidden within the substance;
yet when clearly and definitively illuminated, they point the way to the station of the Sage-King.
Such wondrous goodness does not accrue to those of meager virtue;
auspicious and noble renown does not belong to the unworthy son.
Should one harbor doubt in their heart, they will bring shame upon their own lineage.
Since you have donned the form of a śramaṇa, how could you now abandon it?
Throughout the successive reigns of emperors in ancient times, even before the appearance of the Heavenly Kings,
those who sought the throne in their prime all left the household life in their old age.
King Bimbisāra spoke these words, extensively citing relevant precedents;
there were further bitter and poignant sentiments, expressed through humble and reverent language.
He perceived the Bodhisattva’s intention, which remained as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Maintaining compassion, he gazed silently; with a purified mind, he listened to the instructions.

Chapter Fourteen: Preaching the Dharma for King Bimbisāra The mind is like a heavy, gathering cloud, Desiring to let fall the nectar of immortality.
With a profound and flowing voice, like the pure sound of Brahmā,
and further with eight kinds of gentle and harmonious tones;
preceded by exquisite words, he subdued King Bimbisāra.
The King of Universal Illumination’s intent was upright and pure;
his mind was filled with compassion and reverence.
"Though the King has now arisen in this degenerate, turbid, and chaotic age,"
By skillfully governing himself, he surpasses the kings of antiquity;
seeing the King’s various pure intentions, his inner mind is clear and penetrating.
It is like the clearing of mist and clouds during the day, or like flowers blooming when the sun rises.
"Though one bestows kindness upon a fool, that kindness will never remain with him;
though one performs even a small good deed for a wise person, the favor of that kindness grows ever more profound day by day."
Now I see that the King is most extraordinary; he is not deluded by his royal station.
While those covered by the veil of arrogance and self-indulgence—the lords of lands—are all deluded.
If a wise person acquires wealth, they regard the non-attachment to wealth as their true treasure;
though the body is as transient as a flower in the heat, the wise derive their essential value from it.
“Sentient beings ascend to heaven, attaining great benefit;
the lords of the lands govern with the Dharma of rectitude.
Kings of the True Dharma rule in accordance with principle.”
All people follow what is truly right.
If one possesses wealth and treasures, first examine and grasp their essentials;
if there is further separation, there shall be no heart of resentment afterward.
Just as one extracts butter from curd,
or casts away fermented gruel without any feeling of resentment; so too,
one receives them with hospitality, treating them with the etiquette due to a guest of highest rank.
Opening your heart with profound kindness, out of the spirit of a virtuous friend;
now I shall repay this friendship with my own kindness.
I wish to offer you counsel, so open your mind and listen well.
The lives of all sentient beings are like morning dew;
now I, along with everyone else, shall depart for the next world.
Just as a blazing fire grows even more fierce when it receives clarified butter, so too does this life proceed toward its end.
Even by burning grasses and trees, one is never satisfied;
the mind’s hatred and love arise from ignorance;
all are further deluded, intoxicated by the high drug of madness.
The maladies of old age and decrepitude, the fires of death;
they fiercely burn through the five realms of existence, drowning those who have not attained the outflow-free liberation.
I have now awakened to the power of these raging fires.
Now, wishing to employ skillful means to escape this great calamity,
I therefore abandon my kinsmen and acquaintances;
since sensual desire is like poison, how could I not renounce it?
I have no fear of these venomous serpents;
nor do I fear hail, fierce fires, or swift and violent, evil winds.
Furthermore, I have no fear of murderous bandits with drawn swords.
One only fears the bonds of affection, which lead repeatedly to birth and death.
Those deluded by desire never know satiety;
so it is with the gods, how much more so for the people of the world!
All the world seeks its desires without satiety;
like a blazing fire, it too reaches a point of exhaustion.
Even if one were to obtain all the land within the boundaries of the oceans, it would still not suffice.
Furthermore, greedily seeking passage, they desire to reach the other shore.
In all their searching and striving, there is no satiety;
it is just like the many streams that flow back to the great ocean.
He rained down jewels for seven days until they reached his knees;
he triumphed over the four quarters and ascended as far as the heavens.
His lifespan in the heavens lasted for seven and a half kalpas.
The noble King Mūrdhaja was never satiated by his desires.
There was yet another noble king who enjoyed celestial blessings and emoluments;
at that time, the Lord of Devas fell from his station, fearing the Asuras.
Arrogance then flourished, surpassing even the ranks of the seers;
dwelling in perversity and without satiety, they fell from heaven.
Only those who were full [of merit] became kings and ascended to the heavens.
He obtained celestial maidens, their forms exquisite and wondrous;
yet having offended the divine immortals, his golden jeweled pavilion was destroyed—
consumed by greed, it was instantly turned to ashes.
There was a king named Bhāra who led his troops to ascend to heaven;
returning from heaven, he brought back celestial maidens.
It was because of these celestial maidens that he brought about his own death.
Such beings perish without satiety;
their reputation is base and evil, yet they possess strong bows and swift arrows.
Having renounced the throne, they enter the forest to study the ways of the immortals.
When the mind acts contrary to what is right, one's bodily conduct follows;
by harming others, one’s own body shall likewise perish.
There was a woman named Xian, for whom various kings vied and contended.
Raising an army and leading the multitudes, they face one another in battle.
Because of craving and desire, they give rise to resentment and conflict;
one should abandon craving and desire as if discarding an enemy.
The lineages of various kings harbored resentment, jealousy, and malice;
they killed two hundred and ten Kṣatriyas.
In ancient times, eminent scholars also harbored anger and did harm.
One should abandon evil thoughts, just as a viper sheds its skin.
Speaking of geese and speaking of cranes, they bring about strife;
because of mutual killing and wounding, it reaches even unto hundreds of millions.
Fighting arises from delusion, beginning as something minute;
one should abandon delusion and cast off the disease of one's own ignorance.
In ancient times, two kings fought over the Gandhamādana Grove.
Because of harboring arrogance, they have come to kill and wound one another;
striking with iron clubs, they shatter each other's heads.
You should abandon pride and conceit, which are like a covering cloud.
Furthermore, it is like a warrior, exceedingly strong and swift;
yet because of greed and craving, he seizes the wives of others.
Because of his attachment, he brings about his own ruin.
Just as one fears death, one should abandon attachment to love.
Two asuras perished because of women;
those who crave female beauty will lose their lives upon hearing her voice.
Soaring through the air was Prince Piṇḍola;
these two, craving flavors, both lost their lives.
Long ago, King Eḷamūga, with his trunk, craved fragrance;
By offending the Auspicious Goddess, one brings about ruin and extinction.
In the past, King Śīrṣa enjoyed the pleasure of fine and smooth textures;
through insatiable greed and attachment, his head split apart and he perished.
These people, driven by desire, indulge their six sense-faculties to the utmost;
like the ocean receiving its currents, they are never satisfied.
Even the mouth of the makara fish might yet be filled; [but the senses can never be satiated].
The six sense-faculties receive desires, which are difficult to satisfy.
Such great greed, along with other incalculable afflictions;
when the six sense-faculties are not content, one encounters great hardship.
It may be as Your Majesty says: first indulge the six senses;
who could ever find satiety? You should reflect deeply upon this.
Out of respectful intent, Your Majesty has invited me with the offer of the kingdom.
Behold the throne with discernment: it possesses no pure happiness.
Pure deeds bring a person the experience of supreme joy;
yet after the conditions for that joy have passed, one undergoes great hardship.
Those thick, warm garments are suitable for the fierce cold of winter;
yet when summer heat arrives, they conversely become a source of affliction.
When the hungry obtain food, they consider it a joy of satiety.
If there is one who uses force and compulsion, one will surely encounter great suffering.
It is like a fine lotus pond inhabited by venomous snakes;
or like a grove of flowering trees filled with lions.
A house of gold and jewels is filled with blazing fires;
sovereignty is just like this, which is why I invite you to accept it.
It is like a fish swallowing bait, unaware of the powerful hook.
It is like honey smeared upon the edge of a sharp sword;
the station of a king is like fetters of the seven treasures—
though pleasing to the eye when observed, it brings great suffering to body and mind.
The king’s appearance and adornment are like those of heaven;
he rides the chariot of the kingdom, variegated and firm.
The king’s heavy burden is weightier than a great mountain.
Suffering is like a battle between horses, which those who watch find delight in;
likewise are water, fire, wind, and hail; pestilence, famine, and deprivation;
as well as thieves, robbers, and the violent aggression of enemy nations.
Garrisons stationed on the frontiers suffer from plunder and depletion;
these various hardships weigh most heavily upon the King’s heart.
Day and night he harbors anxiety, and his sleep is restless upon his bed.
He devised expedient means to eliminate the calamities of the state;
yet his mind was universally filled with suspicion, and he did not trust his ministers or subjects;
as if in a land of deadly poison, he accepted food from others.
Even if a king governs countless cities,
his physical presence occupies but one among them;
he sleeps in but a single palace and sits to preside over but a single throne.
Honor and joy are but brief, while anxiety and toil are vast.
Clothing covers but one body; food fills but one frame.
When going out for excursions or sightseeing, the carriage allowed is limited to a single vehicle.
The food and drink of the king are but meager;
for all other labor, he indulges in arrogance and luxury.
The king seeks delight solely in this one thing: the exercise of sovereign power.
This pleasure is likewise mixed with various poisons of suffering;
it is like being situated upon a chariot made of swords—
when one's actions are not clear, they immediately turn back to wound oneself.
It is like a fine house, its exterior adorned with flowers;
yet within it dwell venomous snakes and serpents, filling the interior.
Though it appears pleasing to the eye, contact with it is most poisonous and harmful.
For this reason, I find no pleasure in the royal throne.
For this reason, it is not fitting to accept it;
life and death are difficult to preserve, being like a magical illusion.
How could I know my past karmic counterparts, or where my restless mind would tend?
For this reason, I did not accept the King’s counsel.
When the King spoke of renouncing the household life, he said it was not the right time.
Now listen attentively, and I shall answer for the King.
Eat and drink to your heart's content, harboring no anxieties;
yet death pursues man with many expedients.
The seed of the sugarcane is called Śuddhodana;
O King, you should realize that he was my father-king.
Desiring to escape from suffering, I have therefore renounced the royal throne.
Wishing to establish skillful means and establish wholesome dharmas,
they seek the fearless nirvana as the supreme goal;
may they forever be parted from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Seeking the nectar that can provide lasting security,
one should not take pleasure in meeting with various desires;
it is like wild animals wandering in thirst, seeking water.
Exhausted and parched with thirst, they wander in confusion.
Suddenly encountering a hunter, he blocks their path and pursues them with arrows;
unmoved by their thirst, he will surely kill them.
The world is likewise so; because of the passions of hunger and thirst, it is deluded in myriad ways and does not reckon with the urgency of death.
It seeks pleasure for its own amusement, indulging its desires in food and drink.
When one does not anticipate the completion of an undertaking, there will surely be ruin and failure.
Old age comes and bends the self, like forcibly drawing a bow;
illness harms a person more deeply than a flying arrow.
Death comes pressing upon one's life, like a hunter releasing his encircling net;
when the mind is deluded by folly, how can one wait for the time?
Whether waking or sleeping, whether by day or by night;
Whether on water or on land, for every single person,
life passes away and does not return; it is exceedingly swift,
just like the nature of water entering the mouth of a makara.
The lamp-light of the Dharma is a magnificent brilliance;
augment it with the mind of diligence and increase its ghee.
Those who practice virtue depart with hearts full of joy.
The provisions for the end of life are already fully prepared;
like advancing toward exquisite flowers of most brilliant color,
the man of resolve delights in the good and offers them to the stūpas and images.
If on a later day one sees that the flowers have withered and dried,
having already grasped the essential nature of the flowers, the mind will harbor joy.
If one is a person of clear understanding from childhood onwards;
Harmonizing body and life, one accords with wholesome dharmas.
Beholding one’s own body, already reached the state of decay and old age;
thus regulating one's thoughts, one always harbors joy.
Like a wicked thief who has broken out of prison and fled,
even into the midst of vast wildernesses and great marshes,
or into forests of bamboo and reeds where tigers and wolves roam and dwell;
Deluded and wandering about, driven by the torment of heat and thirst;
five men draw their swords and pursue from behind;
terrified and trembling with fear, he flees and runs away in haste.
Furthermore, there was a fierce and intoxicated elephant that suddenly charged forward,
intending to trample him to death.
Yet the man carried no sword, weapon, or means of combat.
Without provisions for the journey, and lacking even a covering or sandals;
looking out in all four directions, there is forever no one to turn to for refuge;
the mind is clouded with confusion, and nothing can be discerned.
I now purposefully provide this analogy for Your Majesty,
desiring that you understand the course of birth and death.
Your Majesty should understand that birth and death are thus.
To awaken sentient beings is like escaping from a prison;
to recognize the vast wilderness is a metaphor for the three miserable realms;
and to perceive tigers, wolves, and other vicious beasts is the realization of worldly afflictions.
Racing on, utterly exhausted, withered by heat and thirst;
one should know that this is hatred, attachment, and delusion.
With the sharp sword of wisdom, one widely bestows the provisions for the path.
The Great Dharma is a parasol, and the precepts are one’s sandals.
Like that man who lacks these things;
one who does not plant the seeds of virtue is illustrated by this very analogy.
Before one stands a drunken elephant, fierce, violent, and malevolent;
one should realize that the death of the world is just like this.
At that time, there shall be no one to rely upon.
You should rely solely upon this: uphold the precepts and practice virtue.
Your Majesty should turn your mind toward nurturing all people and creatures;
rescue those in peril and relieve those in distress, as if they were your own infants.
Universally harboring a heart of compassion, he regards the people as his own children;
the king should protect the nation just as one guards a palace.
It is like a creature that, through skillful means, is diligent and vigorous.
Fleeing with great speed, one does not encounter a drop of rain;
Great King, you too should likewise flee from the mind,
so as not to encounter evil signs, thereby securing your own deliverance.
Chapter Fifteen: Not So, Ārāḍa. In the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds), Chapter Fifteen: Not So, Ārāḍa: Thus was the Bodhisattva: with broad shoulders and long arms;
moving with calm, deliberate grace, he strode with the gait of a lion.
He went to the arhat to inquire about the essential means for escaping birth and death;
his intention was to break through and destroy the threshold of the gateway to saṃsāra.
From afar he saw the arhat together with his disciples.
They gathered and sat together, discussing the Brahma scriptures.
The Bodhisattva’s virtue was profound, comparable to that of Śakra, Lord of Devas;
they rose to welcome him, inquired after his well-being, and sat with him to converse.
After sitting for a short while, they looked at one another with kind intentions;
the Bodhisattva, with a compassionate mind, comforted the arhat.
The arhat replied:
"Having long been sustained by the transformative influence of the Dharma, I have therefore left the household life; I find no pleasure in honor or glory.
I have torn asunder the web of attachment and its fetters;
strong and courageous, I am like a great elephant."
He renounced his noble title and the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch;
like a wise man who avoids poisoned rice, he cast it aside.
That former wheel-turning monarch was not worth marveling at.
Passing from the vigor of youth into old age, he abandoned his home to enter the forest;
he transferred the royal throne to his crown prince,
just as one discards a withered flower and hands it over to another.
What I now doubt is this: you, O Benevolent One, are youthful, vigorous, and beautiful;
yet the desires of your six senses have not yet reached fulfillment.
You ought to receive vast abundance and enjoy natural splendor and happiness.
If he were to relinquish this noble title, who would not harbor doubts?
If you wish to know whether the Prince’s affairs are indeed as they appear,
you must realize that he will surely become the supreme vessel for the Great Dharma.
"By the virtue of diligence, take up the boat of wisdom;
you must swiftly cross over the deep abyss of birth and death.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva heard the words of Āraṇa.
Smiling and harboring joy, he replied to him, saying:
"My task was not yet accomplished, which is why I came here;
now that you have protected yourself, the task will surely be fulfilled."
It is like suddenly seeing light in the midst of darkness;
it is like a lost person finding someone to lead the way;
it is like one wishing to cross a river encountering a boat for passage.
Therefore, I have come to seek you out to serve as a virtuous teacher.
I hope you will deign to look upon me and grant me your instruction;
if you accept me as your disciple, I shall serve you with the reverence due to a master.
"Regarding the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, by what means should one cross over them?
We pray that you will instruct us with this principle.
Thereupon, Ārāḍa spoke to the Teacher of the World:
“Listen attentively and with discernment to my, the Brahmin’s, Dharma.
Birth and death proceed in succession, revolving and circling;
moving up and down in inversion, just like the turning of a wheel.”
There are eight private matters, termed the "internal laws";
furthermore, there are sixteen matters that cause confusion and doubt.
By these one should know that the person's will is firm.
All worlds arise and cease because of this.
Thus, these five natures are attached to the sixth consciousness;
the seventh is the manas, and the eighth is the state of hesitation.
There are five feelings, and furthermore there are five desires;
one must further awaken to the fact that there are six delusions and disturbances.
To understand these clearly is called awakening to karma.
The Red Immortal shares his station with them, and all together they possess awakening and knowledge.
The Brahmā Heaven is called "Omniscient";
one who thoroughly knows this is said to have the karma of Nirvāṇa.
The roots of birth and death have ripened, entangling us in bonds and attachments;
only by clearly awakening to this is there certainty, for all else remains undecided.

To satiate all those who have long been hungry and empty;

Chapter 25: Subduing the Elephant. From the *Buddha-bhūmi-carita*, Chapter Twenty-five, "Subduing the Elephant. At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the city of Rājagṛha;
as he moved about to bring merit to sentient beings, the earth shook greatly.
The auspicious responses of the Buddhas and their wondrous,
miraculous transformations were all manifested when he was about to enter the city.
At that time, Devadatta harbored a mind of malice and harm.
Perceiving that the Buddha was entering the city, all auspicious omens manifested.
Possessing jealousy, he went swiftly to King Ajātaśatru;
through deceptive inducement, he incited him toward rebellion and evil:
"You usurped your father the King; I shall kill the Buddha.
Together we shall illuminate one another, like the sun and the moon.
He intoxicated the King with false words and the elephant with strong wine.
An elephant, having become intoxicated with wine, roared like the crashing of thunder.
Immediately, the drunken elephant was let loose, charging toward the Buddha;
it was like a violent, dark wind coming to extinguish the lamp of the Buddha.
Like the wind at the end of an eon, which seeks to destroy and annihilate the world;
as powerful as the golden-winged garuḍa, and as wrathful as King Yama—
yet the Buddha’s mind is firm and unshakable, unmoved even by an elephant.
Just as Mount Māra is not moved by the winds of the ocean,
He suddenly came before the Buddha and, upon arrival, bowed with his knees touching the ground;
Subduing his mind and prostrating himself, he was like dust meeting a heavy downpour.
Just as from within crimson clouds, the sunlight shines with brilliant clarity;
like a radiant meteor, it falls upon the summit of a distant mountain.
From the cloud of the *kāṣāya*, he emits the radiance of his right arm.
Radiant light shines upon the great elephant, like the sun upon the Black Mountain.
As the hand of virtue touches the elephant, the elephant immediately awakens;
it is as if a bright torch has appeared, causing the darkness to retreat and shrink away.
The elephant suddenly awoke from its stupor, and its mind immediately found peace;
it was as if by a divine spell, the venom of the viper was instantly dispelled.
The elephant immediately submitted itself, taking refuge at the feet of the Buddha.
The Buddha then manifested a brilliant light, like the sun rising over a mountain ridge.
At that time, he tamed and transformed the intoxicated elephant, instructing it to plant the roots of goodness;
having finished transforming those who were ready for deliverance, he immediately returned to the vihāra.
At that time, within that city, there was a son of noble lineage;

At that time, the wicked Devadatta harbored a heart of intense resentment and anger.

“The jewel has emerged from a great height.

One who lacks satiety runs about in poverty; the one who is content is the object of compassion.
Those who seek liberation should not rely on the clamor of the crowd;
from Śakra, Lord of Devas, downward, all pay homage to those who dwell in solitude.
You all should abandon affection; for in affection one dwells amidst suffering.
One who abandons home yet clings to loved ones is like an old elephant sinking in the mud.
Those whose will is courageous and resolute encounter no obstacles or difficulties in their many undertakings;
though water is inherently soft and weak, its persistent dripping can pierce through stone.
If one drills for fire but rests repeatedly, one will not succeed in producing it;
by drilling with diligence, one eventually attains fire. Thus, the energetic person achieves their goal.
Therefore, one should establish vigor and proceed toward the gate of Nirvāṇa.
Those who deviate from the unconditioned path—be careful not to do so.
Guard your resolve without confusion, and the various evils shall not descend upon you;
the śramaṇa who guards his resolve is a true friend, while he who loses his resolve forgets all that is wholesome.
When one’s will is armored and weapons prepared, no enemy can achieve victory;
when the mind is single-mindedly clad in the armor of virtue, the afflictions of worldly toil cannot prevail.
Those who apply themselves with focused concentration clearly comprehend the cycle of birth and death in the world.
Therefore, one should fix the mind; when the mind is fixed, suffering does not arise.
If one wishes to cross a flowing stream, one relies on bridges and rafts;
if one wishes to cross all suffering, a fixed mind is the supreme boat.
"You who possess wisdom and detachment, I now manifest these worldly dharmas for your sake;
by having them, one attains liberation, for that which lies outside the Dharma is not cherished.
Do not think of this as merely 'leaving home,' for it is armor, a potent medicine, and a sharp tool."
As a boat carries one across a flowing river, wisdom carries one across birth and death.
Therefore, always listen to the Dharma; you should follow the instructions of the Dharma.
Those with the vision of wisdom see what is right; those without wisdom are blind and dark.
If the mind dwells together with worldly afflictions, one will never attain liberation;
those who earnestly seek deliverance must diligently eliminate these afflictions.
The śramaṇa studies to discipline the mind and remove the intent of negligence.
The heart of the Lord of Devas is harmonious and joyful, while the asuras find no joy.
I instruct you in what is good; you should practice it with diligence.
By employing manifold skillful means, I shall lead you to nirvāṇa.

In the midst of tranquil mountain crags, within forest thickets or empty hermitages, train your mind in meditative concentration; do not harbor regrets after I have departed. A skilled physician exhausts all medical arts, compounding various medicines; yet even he cannot restore life to one whose time has come. Thus, when the end of life arrives, there is no means of escape. Therefore, you should practice with diligence while I am still here. If you can cultivate the Way in this life, you shall surely attain the fruit of Arhatship. Once you have attained that fruit, you will forever be free from birth and death. You must strive with vigor and never slacken. If you fail to achieve it now, you will suffer later. Once the body is cast aside, you will fall into the three evil realms. There, you will undergo immeasurable suffering for a hundred thousand kalpas. Even if you were to encounter a Buddha, you would find it difficult to meet him again. If you do not meet a Buddha, how could you ever hear the Dharma? If you do not hear the Dharma, how could you ever know the Path? If you do not know the Path, how could you ever attain liberation? Therefore, you must practice with vigor while I am still here. Do not wait until I have passed away before you begin. If you wait until I am gone, you will repent too late. You must exert yourself now, without delay. If you can cultivate the Way in this life, you shall surely attain the fruit of Arhatship.
