The patient takes the medicine and recovers, yet the physician does not take it himself.
The guide leads correctly, and those who follow suffer no distress;
those who deviate and lose their way incur harm because they disregard the danger.
"I have already expounded the Four Noble Truths for you;
let those who harbor doubts now ask, for this is precisely the time.
When the Buddha had thus instructed them, his disciples remained silent and spoke no word.
Ānanda, knowing their thoughts, spoke among the great assembly:
"The sun may be made cool, and the moon may be made hot;
yet these Four Noble Truths are true and real, and can never be contravened."
The truth of suffering is oppressed by suffering; where there is craving, there is ultimately suffering.
This is what all Buddhas have taught: the truth of cessation is the extinction of craving.
The ambrosia of the Eightfold Noble Path leads to nirvāṇa, which is characterized by quiescence.
The assembly of śramaṇas has awakened; after the Buddha, they shall deliver others from calamity.

Among those gathered who have not yet crossed over—whether old or young, newly entered upon the Path—the Buddha has briefly described the arhat, like a flash of lightning illuminating the way in the darkness.
"He who has already attained liberation, Who has crossed over birth and death;
The multitude together harbors grief and resentment— How could the Master’s passing be so swift?
The Buddha heard Anuruddha Speak such words of true and correct reality.
Desiring to strengthen the resolve of the assembly, he spoke these words out of compassion:
“Even if one possesses a lifespan lasting for an eon, it must ultimately come to an end;
since I have perfected the practice of giving, what use have I for long life?”
In the world and among the heavens, those whom I ought to deliver—half have been delivered and half have been shown the Way;
thus the turning of the Dharma-teaching has become established.
You all should practice awakening and self-restraint; there is no need to pursue thoughts of me.
But diligently speak of skillful means, so as not to encounter the pain of separation.
With the lamp of wisdom dispel the darkness, realizing that the world has nothing firm or enduring;
at the end of life, the heart shall be filled with joy, like the removal of a grievous illness.
The wise are liberated from misfortune and decline; they stay far away from wicked people.
Having attained the relinquishing of these two afflictions, on what basis could they harbor sorrow?
You all must diligently cultivate goodness, for all shall eventually die.
I am entering the city of Nirvāṇa; the time for my arrival is now near.
Here, I relinquish the formations of life—this is my final word.
Thereupon the Buddha contemplated the first dhyāna, free from desire.
Arising from the first dhyāna, he contemplates the second dhyāna,
and thus proceeds through all four;
in this manner, traversing them completely, he moves back and forth through the nine dhyānas, exhausting their sequence both in direct and reverse order.
The World-Honored One, God among Gods, returned to the first dhyāna;
rising from the first dhyāna, he again contemplated up to the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, the Buddha contemplated with thorough discernment, traversing the dhyānas both in reverse and in forward order.
Furthermore, arising once more from this state, he slightly stirred his mind;
then, relinquishing the formations of life, he suddenly entered the city of Nirvāṇa.
As soon as the Buddha relinquished the formations of life, the earth shook in six ways.
In the sky there is a great torch, like the conflagration at the end of an eon;
Great fires arise from the four quarters, like the asuras;
They burn the celestial forests, trees, and marshes—this is called the bliss of the exhaustion of craving.
Torrential rain and hail swirl as dust; lightning flashes like spewing flames.
The entire world is like a great conflagration, and the roar of thunder is most terrifying.
Sudden, violent winds and mist arise, breaking trees and toppling mountain crags.
Just like the winds at the end of an eon, which cause infinite destruction and injury;
the bright sun loses its luster, and the stars and moon are dark and dim;
when both the sun and moon lose their light, they are as if smeared with mud.
Though the sun and moon shine together, the darkness is not dispelled;
one cannot distinguish east from west, and day from night cannot be known.
When the World-Honored One is shrouded in obscurity, even the rivers flow upstream.
Beside the Bodhi tree, in the twin groves, sorrowful flowers fell;
the waters of the Ganges all grew hot, like the boiling broth in a cauldron;
the twin trees withered for his sake, bending down to cover the body of the World-Honored One.
The five-headed great dragon kings, their bodies slackened with grief, gazed upon the Buddha with feverish distress; weeping, their eyes were all bloodshot.
Immediately they exhaled hot breath, a stifling venom beyond description.
It burns and heats the throat, like the grave affliction of vomiting up one's own heart.
Contemplating that the entire world is impermanent, one should admonish oneself to forcibly remove sorrow;
for the king of one’s own mind leads its retinue, one must remember the Dharma and cease weeping.
The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, Having understood the Way, their minds were harmonized and settled;
Silent and without weeping, they took pity on the world’s arising and ceasing.
The foremost *Gandharva* spirits, And the powerful Naga kings;
The devas who revere the Dharma were filled with sorrow, their compassion choking the void of space.
Enveloped everywhere by grief, they ran about in agitation, moved by lamentation;
the great cries of these various beings filled the entire world.
Māra has already attained his desire, and his evil hordes rejoice;
they dance and brandish drums that thunder like peals of lightning, emitting all manner of great roars.
With loud cries, they proclaim their commands:
"Our Lord, the mighty foe, has perished; from this day forth, who else will be able to transgress his boundaries?
The Buddha’s tree of virtue has fallen, like the tusks of a great elephant broken, like the crags of a high mountain shattered, like the horns of a great bull fallen off.
The Buddha now relinquishes his body and life;
all the devas and humans of the world have nothing left to turn to for refuge.
They have lost their protector in this way, like a sky without the sun, or like a kingdom that has lost its granaries and treasuries.
Like a flower pond struck by frost, where all the blossoms are withered and damaged;
when the World-Honored One relinquished his body and life, becoming silent and hidden in *nirvāṇa*,
all sentient beings of form lost their vitality and splendor.
Chapter Thirty: Praising the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). At that time, from the midst of the sky, a celestial palace of precious jewels shone forth;
drawn by a chariot of a thousand elephants, it hung suspended above.
With a heart of deep reverence, [the deity] gazed intently at the Buddha as he lay with his body resting, having relinquished his life.
Filled with emotion, he sighed in lamentation and spoke these words:
"Abiding within the great cycle of birth and death, all things are impermanent;
What first arises appears flourishing, but ultimately decays, diminishes, and perishes."
Turning toward what is desired brings forth manifold sufferings;
when all sufferings are utterly extinguished, there is the supreme bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The various kinds of firewood of birth and death are burned away until nothing remains.
The smoke of the virtue of his wisdom’s flame spreads throughout the heavens and the world;
yet the waters of impermanence suddenly arrive, extinguishing the Buddha’s magnificent radiance—
just as a wild, fierce fire is suddenly met by a great torrential rain.
Furthermore, there was a celestial seer, Whose mind was keen, virtuous, and well-disciplined;
Dwelling in the Pure Abode palaces, Pure and having eliminated all desires.
Seeing the Buddha, he felt profound love and reverence, Weeping like falling rain from the clouds.
With a mind as heavy as Mount Sumeru, he then uttered these words:
"In this world, there is never anyone who is born and does not die;
from time immemorial, there has never been anyone who is born and remains forever."
Having thoroughly investigated and mastered the superior, middling, and inferior, there is nothing he does not know with certainty;
yet even he cannot escape this [suffering], so how could others remain forever?
This great guide of the world has departed from the false and shown the true path.
The eye of wisdom is supreme; it observes the world’s fluctuations between high and low.
When such worldly wisdom is extinguished, one will return to and follow false guidance;
like a blind man without eyes, one loses the way on the level and upright path.
"The disciple with the foremost divine eye, named Ānanda;
his likes and dislikes have been exhausted, his toil ended, and birth-and-death severed.
Having seen that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the world shall fall into darkness."
With his faculties stilled and his mind extinguished, he then uttered these words of praise:
"Abiding within the great cycle of birth and death, the meaning of wisdom cannot be fully expressed;
the world is like a mist, empty and vanishing in an instant."
The vajra of impermanence strikes the precious Sumeru of the Buddhas;
suddenly it crumbles and collapses, now falling to the ground.
How fragile is birth in this world—there is not a single thing upon which one can rely.
Vague and insubstantial, lacking any firm core; restless and agitated, they scatter as soon as they meet.
The law of universal destruction is like a dream, devoid of self or "mine";
the Buddha, the Lion, can subdue it, and the elephant of affliction falls of its own accord.
How could those who have not yet attained the Path of the Stream-enterer not fear this?
Beholding the world as something unreliable, like a cluster of morning dew or foam,
the Buddha is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Great Pillar of Vajra.
Suddenly it collapses to the ground—where then is its power?
Six kinds of growth produce five branches; from one sprout come five fruits.
Watered together as three stalks, the laboring mind is truly difficult to fell.
The elephant of the Buddha’s great power Sudden breaks down the tree of afflictions;
Crushing it until nothing remains, Only then does it fall to the ground.
The Thousand-Eyed One wields the vajra, And the Lord of Devas receives the timely rain.
Established in the True Dharma, he extinguished suffering and attained cool serenity.
His reputation for virtue grew ever more vast and wide, universally covering the world;
yet the Teacher of all sages and worthies has now entered into tranquil parinirvāṇa.
His fame and virtue are all-pervading, and the subtle Dharma is refreshingly moist;
like autumn rain, the waters of the Dharma fill the rivers and streams.
The Celestial Master extends his saving protection, while the King of his own mind serves as his retinue.
Bestowing upon them the Way of Non-action, he withdraws his presence like the setting sun.
He raises clouds and sends down this rain; in autumn and winter, there are snow, rain, and frost.
Amidst the blazing intensity of a raging fire, nothing can extinguish it.

Just as when a sacrifice is finished and the fire goes out, so now the fire of the Teacher of the Gods has suddenly been extinguished and stilled, leaving no light; the world is plunged forever into deep darkness.
Those who sought liberation have lost their hope, and having failed their original vow, they are deprived of joy.
His virtuous fame and reputation spread abroad, pervading and filling the ten directions.
Cherishing the four immeasurables and great compassion, he pitied all beings as if they were his own infants;
there was none who did not receive his kindness—how can he now pass away into such silent extinction?
Having attained the wondrous path of non-attachment, the source from which all Buddhas arise;
possessing unimpeded wholesome dharmas, he realized awakening in profound stillness.
With the supernormal power of light-footedness, he awakened to the fact that the body is the cessation of suffering.
For this reason, with swiftness, he cast off his body and dwelt in peace within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
He removed all darkness of mind, like the thousand rays of the sun;
he extinguished the defilement of lust in the mind, as rain settles the dust upon the earth.
No longer shall they encounter manifold sufferings, nor be oppressed by afflictions;
having already crossed the vast and boundless ocean, deep and shoreless.
Arising in the world to manifest its glory, they destroy all bitter poisons and calamities.
Compassionate toward the world, he seeks to lead those who desire quiescence.
With a magnificent radiance of sublime marks, he is as serene as the Brahma King;
possessing universal great wisdom, he is the Teacher of gods and humans in the world.
Transforming sentient beings through goodness, refining them from afflictions and freeing them from evil;
increasing all virtues day and night like the waxing of the new moon,
constantly nurturing every merit until its fame is vast and universal.
If he already understood this while living as a householder, how much more so after he has renounced the home?
In the distant past, he made a vow: "I shall wage war against the afflictions;
out of compassion for those who are poor and lowly, I vow to fulfill their every wish."
With a mind of equanimity, the Buddha eats without rejecting coarse or poor food;
nor does he have any attachment to refined or delicious flavors.
He practices giving that is difficult to relinquish—what others are unable to do.
He does not receive anything from others, nor does he seek any personal gain.
His marks of excellence and great renown arise spontaneously like an echo;
having extensively gathered the good intentions of the multitude, he listens with resolute attention to what is wholesome.
Therefore, he manifests physical marks and graceful features, so that those who behold him have the three impurities extinguished;
his speech establishes the Dharma and Vinaya, long increasing the goodness of sentient beings.
By practicing the mark of patience, he makes it manifest, acting as an enemy to the afflictions.
Though one accumulates immeasurable merit, one cannot escape impermanence.
The rewards received for the merit accumulated in this life are without limit;
one will certainly attain the True Path, just as a fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Showing the path of goodness to sentient beings, he utterly clears away the forest of afflictions;
he controls all those who are bound and attached within birth and death.
Having abandoned the eight [liberations] and the five destinies, he beholds the three realms of existence.
Having struck down the three and exhausted the three, one thereby attains the purity of the three eyes.
Concealing one and awakening to one, one reaches the single state up to the sevenfold weightiness;
dispersing them so that nothing remains, one then vows to the unobstructed.
Filling the world with ambrosia, his words severed all anger;
he transformed sentient beings through goodness, even those in the world who were difficult to enlighten.
He constantly planted the roots of myriad virtues, never inflicting evil upon the wicked.
He raises the banner of the True Dharma throughout all worlds.
At Deer Park he turns the wheel of Dharma, bringing universal joy to the world;
he accomplishes all liberations and purifies those who cherish themselves.
Seeing what has never been seen before, he is universally in accord with purity;
he awakens to all things difficult to awaken to, and to all dharmas never before awakened to.
He proclaims to the world its impermanence, and that whatever is born is inevitably accompanied by suffering.
He proclaims to the world that there is no self; there is no "other," yet long delusions persist.
He raises the banner and pennant of the Dharma to shatter the high mountain of arrogance, like a pillar of the seven treasures collapsing amidst a sacrificial rite.
Not harboring resentment when reviled face-to-face, nor finding pleasure in praise;
weary of birth yet receiving celestial blessings, one seeks through skillful means the state of non-birth.
Having crossed the ocean of birth and death oneself, one further delivers all others.
Having personally attained awakening through wisdom, you further awaken sentient beings.
Like clouds moistening at the time of dawn, like flowers in the mountains, forests, and marshes;
your liberation from views is like the rising sun, and you bestow upon them right view.
Though born into the world, one is not stained by worldly affairs;
traversing the perilous paths of the world, one’s destination is not the same as others’.
The mind has never committed a transgression; even while on the path of goodness, one strives for cessation.
The entire world encounters hardship, Lacking any reliance or support, a source of sorrow.
Ignorance obscures their eyes, And they ultimately have no foresight;
They do not contemplate establishing skillful means To seek the essential way out of birth and death.
The sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death Oppress the world; none may escape them.
Only the Buddha can save from suffering And bestow upon them the nectar of immortality.
In the past, the armies of the celestial Māras Could not defeat the Teacher of Gods.
By the natural power of impermanence, impermanence suddenly overcomes him.
With his ears, the World-Honored One hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world system;
by means of his supernormal powers, he ascends and descends as far as the Brahma heavens.
He awakens to the mental activities of sentient beings, down to those in the Avīci Hell;
he clearly and thoroughly perceives all the arising and ceasing of birth and death.
From his initial birth as a Teacher of Gods, he has undergone every cycle of transmigration.
Recalling this clearly as if seeing it face to face, he has exhausted the source of the outflows of birth and death.
Possessing the wisdom of the six supernormal powers and fully endowed with the certainty of awakening,
he now completely relinquishes all attachments, casting off his body and remaining only for the duration of his final lifespan.
The world flows through birth and death in the stream of craving; who shall preach the Dharma to bring it to rest?
The worldly are deluded and lack wisdom; who shall awaken them so that their ignorance is extinguished?
It is like a chariot without a driver, or a boat on the rivers and seas that has lost its captain.
When one is gravely ill and separated from a skilled physician, how can one sustain oneself?
Just as it is said that when separated from sincerity and trust, one seeks wisdom without the factors of awakening;
or as a king who has lost his finery and ornaments, yet practices virtue and cannot endure humiliation.
Having already abandoned these four matters, his merit does not manifest;
now that the Buddha has departed from the world, there is no one to rescue those who find it difficult to achieve their goals.
It is like the fifth or sixth month of summer, pure and free of wind and clouds.
The fierce yang energies clash and burn, Reaching even to all insects and creatures.
Those sentient beings who were ready for deliverance Now shall universally encounter this calamity;
The World-Honored One has relinquished his life-span— How singularly bitter and painful this is!
At that time, the deva, harboring a heart of compassion and pitying him, spoke these words:
"Because lust, anger, and delusion have been thinned, he praises the Teacher and reviles birth-and-death.
As for the disciples who have not yet attained liberation, they wail and weep in bitter grief."
Those who had already attained liberation carefully calculated the passing of time as the signs of decline appeared.
The sound of the news spread throughout all the kingdoms;
the Mallas of Kuśinagara, moved by both grief and courage, swiftly rushed forth and gathered together at the space between the twin śāla trees.
Lamenting and leaping, he threw himself against the wall, praising the Buddha’s virtues in various ways;
his voice was most piteous, like a flock of cranes encountering a hawk.
Seeing that the Buddha had lost his radiance and entered nirvana beyond recovery, he fell into despair.
They wailed in unison with voices of grief, writhing like fish on parched land.
Seeing the Buddha suddenly lying down, his limbs all stretched out straight;
it was as if a Wheel-Turning King had passed away, and there were no lands that did not cry out in lamentation.
Countless people emerged from the city to go to where the Buddha was;
men and women, old and young alike, were overwhelmed by grief and frantic with distress.
Some tore their clothes apart, while others, moved by intense pain, bit their own lips.
Some tore out their own hair, clawing and tearing at their faces until they were disfigured.
Furthermore, countless others, overcome with anguish, threw themselves down;
beating their breasts and crying out toward heaven, they extolled the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues.
"Alas! Teacher of Gods and Humans, upon whom all sentient beings rely;
why do you abandon us so swiftly? Forever cut off, there shall be no further hope."
The great assembly wept with grief, each doing what they could;
the king of the Mallas, in agonizing pain, cried out and sighed:
"The Teacher who awakened to the Dharma and realized the world now lies prostrate and shall not rise again."
Just as when a great army has disbanded, its mighty banner no longer appears;
having accomplished what was to be done, and awakened to that which a Buddha awakens to—
he who was like an eye for the world now lies in sudden, eternal sleep.
The Buddha is the bridge for crossing over suffering, used to ferry one across the swift-flowing river;
when that great bridge is suddenly destroyed, by what means can one cross over the pains?
The light of the Buddha’s wisdom shines forth, its heart-illumination radiant with the glow of diligence.
In the past, when the Buddha-sun appeared and shone, it caused heaven and earth to be universally illuminated.
Now its light has vanished and it is hidden away within the great mountain of non-action;
the world shall surely return to its former state, suddenly entering the long-lasting darkness of decay.
Some wailed with piteous moans or spoke in delirium; some gazed fixedly with hearts full of despair;
some wept until their voices were spent, while others covered their faces with the ground.
As sentient beings harbored the poison of affliction, the forms of their weeping were manifold.
There was none who did not harbor longing and yearning, their hearts pained and trembling with anxiety.
Thereupon, with a palanquin adorned with the seven treasures and ivory,
the various *rishi* (powerful men) carried the Buddha and placed him upon the precious palanquin.
A variety of rare flowers and incense, along with all manner of wondrous things;
the Mallas wailed as they made offerings to the Buddha’s relics.
There were young maidens of noble lineage, their forms graceful and their hands delicate.
They hold canopies of the seven treasures, as exquisite as celestial silks;
they adorn jeweled parasols with bright pearls, or hold dangling jewel-strings;
some grasp jeweled whisks and fans, making offerings to the Buddha’s relics.
The Mallas bore the litter, their eyes red with weeping;
from the sky came the sound of thunder, pleasing and delightful to the ears.
The devas scattered various *manojña* flowers, falling continuously like pouring rain.
The devas let flowers fall upon the ground, their brilliance appearing as if they had just blossomed.
The devas filled the void of space, making offerings of various jewels to the Buddha;
they uttered verses of poignant lamentation, sighing in admiration of the Buddha’s virtues.
The various goddesses who enjoy music sprinkled sandalwood fragrant juice;
scattering necklaces and precious robes, they made offerings to the Buddha’s relics.
The Mallas carried the palanquin, leading it to the center of the city.
Devas and humans paid respectful homage, weeping with longing remembrance;
with silks, brocades, precious banners, and streamers, they adorned the city walls;
with flowers, incense, and music, they made offerings to the Honored Relics.
Carrying a precious palanquin as an offering, they departed through the western gate of the city;
having reached the west side of the city, they crossed the flowing waters of the River Jambu.
Ascending to the foot of a sweet-smelling tree, they used various kinds of fragrant wood.
They piled up a great heap of firewood, as well as various kinds of incense,
various kinds of fragrant flowers, and diverse types of unguents;
each person took hold of a torch, desiring to burn the Buddha’s pyre.
The three kinds of firewood for the Buddha’s pyre were piled up, yet the flames refused to ignite;
all the people were filled with doubt, not knowing the cause.
Mahākāśyapa was not far away; harboring compassion, he went to see the Buddha.
At that time, because of this, they blew together but the fire would not ignite.
Then Kāśyapa arrived quickly; having paid homage to the Buddha’s funeral pyre, the wood of the Buddha’s pyre spontaneously ignited at that very moment.
Defilements do not harm the Buddha; now he is consumed by fire.
Although his flesh and body are entirely spent, his bones remain as they were, unburnt.
At that time, the Mallas extinguished the fire by pouring milk upon it.
The bones were washed with fragrant water, and the śarīras were placed in a golden jar.
Just as in the past when the Lord of Devas sought to burn Mount Vajra,
because his merit was so great, fire could not consume it.
Now, even with this great blazing fire, it cannot burn the Buddha’s bone;
as the Mallas passed it from one to another, they spoke this analogy to one another:
"Born from the four immeasurable minds, it extinguishes the fire of lustful desire."
The Venerable One’s bones are tranquil and cool, yet our hearts burn with anguish.
Though the devas and powerful rishis could not overcome the Buddha’s body,
now that it has suddenly met with impermanence, I shall carry it forth.
The Buddha’s power is peerlessly strong, and his voice resounds throughout the ten directions;
how could he then be so dazed as to place it within a golden jar?
The Buddha’s brilliance is like the sun, yet he has never been conceited.
Encountering the fire of impermanence, only their spiritual remains are left behind;
with the vajra-pestle of wisdom, they shatter the formidable mountain of afflictions;
meeting suffering, they do not abandon patience, their minds firm and unshakable.
Having severed the root of all suffering, he has extinguished it so that he shall no longer receive a body;
such a wondrous being has found eternal end within the flames.
Wherever the Malla ever went, his strength would subdue others until they wept.
Those who came to seek refuge and submission, he could comfort and satisfy so that they were gladdened.
Even when encountering hardships, relying on his strength, he never wept;
yet mindful of the Buddha’s virtue and compassion, he wept as he carried the śarīra.
Possessing powerful strength and martial equipment, his will was refined yet harbored arrogance;
weeping, he returned to the city, where his mind became humble and his pride was removed.
He presented banners and canopies to the great hall and offered a high seat made of the seven precious gems.
Placing the *śarīra* upon it, they all paid homage and made offerings.

Chapter 31: The Division of the *Śarīra* by the Eight Kings. In the *Buddha-benxing-jing*, Chapter Thirty-one: The Division of the *Śarīra* by the Eight Kings. The Mallas, moved by grief, remained within the royal palace;
they made offerings to the venerable *śarīra* for several days in this manner.
The seven neighboring kings each immediately dispatched envoys;
all arriving at one and the same time, they gathered beneath the city walls.
Each delivered his king’s message, and the Mallas heard one another.
They all expressed their reverence and sought to obtain a portion of the relics.
The Mallas replied:
"The Buddha passed away in our kingdom; we shall make offerings to the relics ourselves and cannot grant any to you."
At that time, the envoys from various kingdoms consulted one another several times;
the Mallas, lifting the śarīra, likewise relied on their great strength.
The envoys refused to return, saying, "We must dispatch it by means of our sovereign power."
Each harbored thoughts of pride, having no intention of sharing the relics.
The envoys returned and reported this; each king then conceived his own resolve.
They immediately raised their armies, which fanned out like the wind and reached the city.
With countless hosts of troops, they surrounded the city of Malla;
as the army advanced toward the city, it was like a torrential downpour.
The people retreated into the depths of the city, none of whom were without fear.
The multitude of people was so vast that the city could not contain them;
the armies of the seven kings, with the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses,
shook the city walls, and the people trembled like waves.
Thereupon the armies of the seven kings were each stationed in their respective divisions;
the warriors, elephants, and horses were highly trained and exceedingly brave.
Thus the various kings, according to their strength, each made diligent preparations.
The fourfold battle arrays— elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—
were likewise deployed by the mighty warriors; defensive weapons were arrayed upon the city walls,
the moats and ditches were repaired, and all the city gates were barred.
Even though they have all established great banners upon their military formations,
none among the common people within the realm fail to harbor fear.
At that time, the seven kings consulted with one mind.
Each accompanied by countless multitudes, fully equipped with sharp and精良 weapons and armor;
like the seven stars of the lunar mansions appearing together in the night,
the armies of the seven kings arrived simultaneously at the foot of the city wall.
The great multitude raised yellow dust, which filled and blocked the eyes of the people;
the stench of the elephant’s breath clogged their nostrils so they could not breathe;
the sounds of drums, horns, and conchs deafened their ears so that nothing could be heard.
The women and all the young children were struck with terror and their complexions turned pale;
they set up incendiary devices and melted copper and iron into boiling liquid;
all donned helmets and armor, standing ready to advance into battle with their weapons.
Elephants and horses were all clad in armor, drawn up in formation to face the battle;
the *malla* warriors risked their very lives, having no thought for dividing the relics.
Within the city, everyone was urged to hasten, taking up weapons and ascending the walls to fight.
The Mallas, with one heart, were determined not to retreat in battle;
they all took their positions atop the city walls, amidst the watchtowers and defensive bulwarks,
watching the kings outside and their countless military hosts.
The army stirred up a display of martial prowess, shouting and crying out all at once;
their simultaneous clamor shook heaven and earth.
Drawing and brandishing their swords, they flashed and dazzled like the light of the sun and sky.
Some leaped and ran with great vigor, seeking to reach the city with swift agility.
Seeing the Mallas, the enemy troops tightened their belts and made themselves ready;
they were determined to engage in battle, showing no intention whatsoever of retreating.
Each bidding farewell to their wives and children as they advance to battle;
the wives and children of the warriors harbor fear and tremble like waves.
Furthermore, those who have parents feel a heart of love and longing for their sons.
Seeing his son clad in armor, about to go forth to the battlefield, they wept and wailed aloud;
they prayed to the trees and invoked the deities.
Seeing their parents’ grief, the son’s heart was filled with lingering doubt.
Some women remained silent, harboring grief and distress;
others took up celestial bows and arrows, weeping as they blocked them from fighting.
Seeing their wives and children wailing, their hearts became fierce, resolute, and courageous.
Seizing the bow and arrows, he was determined to fight without hesitation;
the various strongmen, relying on their own prowess, were resolute in their desire for battle.
Like a viper hidden within a vessel, they harbored a fury that burned with intensity.
Their minds were all resolved, certain they would fight without hesitation;
the seven kings likewise made their preparations, and the battle was about to commence.
All had long since prepared the fourfold armies.
With elephant troops and cavalry, and a multitude of chariot and infantry forces,
there was a brahmin of noble lineage named Gandhabba.
By nature broad-minded, wise, and deeply compassionate, he exhorted the kings with these words of counsel:
"Observe the majesty and power of kings, equipped with sharp weapons, swords, and martial gear;
desiring to subdue powerful enemies, they seek to utterly extinguish their form, strength, and life.
Those who dwell within their cities to defend themselves cannot easily achieve victory."
Within the city, the Mallas have attained unity;
with one mind and purpose they now stand encircled. Their intent is surely to achieve victory;
we pray that the Great Kings will deign to turn back their magnificent might.
Examine those within the city who follow the good and are well-disciplined;
all the kings know this fully—what offense has been committed that you should inflict such suffering?
That which is restrained by force will surely bear fruit; victory is not achieved alone.
When one falls into an encirclement, skillful means overcome the external enemy;
A venomous snake preserves its own life by entering its hole and concealing its form;
If someone reaches in with their hand for no reason, they may be stung and suffer death or injury.
Perceiving themselves as possessing power, they can shake others and strike them with fear;
gathering together, they enter the city and take refuge, firmly establishing their defenses.
Though their strength was originally weak, upon entering the city, they become possessed of great power.
Just as a lamp on the verge of extinction blazes up again when supplied with oil and fuel,
so too, if within that city there are those who possess the precepts and are truly divine,
the external enemies will naturally disperse and fall apart because of the weight of their virtuous discipline.
Just as in the past, King Choung-yuan exhausted his military strength;
yet King Ch'ing-ming, possessing virtue, conquered external and powerful enemies.
The kings of former times expanded their territories through force; [but now, through virtue, he has surpassed them].
Seeking to indulge their passions, they spread their fame to the farthest reaches;
yet when the king’s term of office suddenly passes, it is like an ox drinking ice-cold water—
the various kings have all gone by, while the lands and territories remain.
Therefore, one should reflect deeply upon the true principles of the world:
by employing skillful means to bring about harmony, one gains the precious relics.
To overcome an enemy through the force of arrows brings about the birth of a vengeful foe who returns with hostility.
He achieves victory through harmony and gentleness, never again giving rise to retaliation.
Though his words may seem foolish and base, and though there is truly nothing in them worth adopting,
the kings possess great and powerful strength, capable of subduing even minor adversaries.
"Just as one honors a revered teacher, so those who uphold the Dharma are supreme;
now you should call to mind your teacher and practice the teaching of patience.
At that time, that brahmin exhausted all that he knew within his own being.
With gentle and harmonious true words, he admonished the kings with a compassionate heart.
He caused all those kings—who possessed fierce and haughty minds—to turn back and submit.
Thereupon, the kings, having complied, replied to the brahmin in submissive terms:
"What you have said is timely and appropriate; you understand expedient means with harmony and compliance.
The excellent principles you have now expounded are profound and sincere, persisting from beginning to end.
You should examine us closely and realize in your heart the power of the Dharma."
Whatever the heart desires and seeks, one does not labor to indulge in worldly things.
Whether by aspiration or by power, or through anger, resentment, and hatred;
those who have already contended and are now fighting, or those who shall face each other in battle.
"As our intention now is purely to seek the virtues of a Buddha;
we carry weapons to seek for relics, not out of greed for the kingdom’s wealth and treasures.
The ancient and valiant Malla, full of pride, replied with these great words:
"In the battle for the Immortal Grove, the dead and wounded are beyond counting.
The Buddha has spread his teaching throughout the world to remove toil and extinguish arrogance;
why do you not become a Buddha, instead cherishing this precarious and fragile life?"
In ages past, various kings were deluded by the beauty of noble women;
they raised armies to wage war and punish one another, and countless kings perished.
The Buddha’s teaching truly transforms the world, extinguishing the intentions of greed and lust.
Yet I do not strive for Buddhahood; why cherish this precarious and fragile life?
In days past, there were brothers who, out of folly and envy, gave rise to resentment and strife;
they turned upon one another with mutual injury and slaughter until none remained.
The Buddha has arisen and manifested in the world, extinguishing the hearts of ignorance and envy;
why do you not become a Buddha, yet cling to your life and refuse to fight?
In the past, the powerful wrestler, harboring resentment and bound by hatred;
We have taken up arms, desiring to exterminate the entire lineage of kings;
yet now that a Buddha has appeared in the world, able to eliminate all hatred and harm—
for his sake, why should we cherish these lives?
In the past, there was a man named Huashangzi, Known as the Ten-Headed Spirit;
Firmly attached to sensual desires, He lost his life because of them.
When the Buddha appeared in the world, He untied all fetters and attachments.
For the sake of the Buddha, why do we cling to this body and life?
In the past, foolish people were like insects writhing in the water of delusive contention;
because their ignorance was so rampant, they sought to kill one another.
The Buddha has appeared in the world to eliminate all ignorance;
for the sake of the Buddha, why do we, out of deluded attachment, cling to this body?
Since time immemorial, the ignorant have failed to realize that what they dispute is but foul and impure.
There is not a single thing of lasting substance; mutual harm is beyond calculation.
Since the Buddha has appeared to remove the world’s afflictions, we act for the sake of the Buddha;
we shall fight against Yama—how could we doubt this worldly battle?
"Our minds are firm and upright; we shall never doubt in battle.
Send laborers into the city to the place where the Mallas are, and with all your heart employ skillful means to explain our sincere intentions."
Since we place our trust and reliance in your benevolence, you must grant us a single combat.
We shall aim our sharp arrows with focused intent and engage in battle;
meanwhile, may we hear your exposition of the sublime Dharma and your words of perfect truth.
Within his heart, the poisonous venom of hatred was immediately extinguished;
like a serpent charmed by incantation, its lethal poison was destroyed without remainder.
At that time, the brahmin, having received the command of the various kings;
He immediately proceeded into the city and went to where the Mallas were.
Desiring to see those Mallas who were esteemed and possessed of power,
he approached them with an attitude of humility and respect, proclaiming the royal command:
"The armies of the kings outside the city / All have their weapons strictly prepared;
/ Pierced by spears and clad in jeweled armor, / They shine brilliantly like the sun in the sky.
/ They resolve to raise their voices in unison / To exhaust all their martial might."
With a mind as courageous as a lion, he opened his eyes wide and gazed toward the city.
He rubbed and polished his bow, which was already fully prepared and inlaid with gold and jewels;
his courage remained tireless, and day and night he did not remove his armor.
Suddenly he resolved his mind and called to mind the Buddha’s compassionate and luminous Dharma;
through the labor of yielding according to the marks of righteousness, he did not doubt or fear combat.
Without contending for territory, he has come to the foot of this city.
Without arrogance, greed, or stinginess, and without coming with anger or resentment;
because of reverence for the Buddha’s merit, I have come to this place of yours.
Since you, guest, have come with virtuous purpose, it is fitting that you, host, should receive me with respect.
The Buddha is the teacher of all; we alike revere and serve him.
Desiring to make offerings to his relics, we have come to this city.
Since we are brothers in the Dharma, we pray that you will share the relics with us.
One should cause sentient beings in great numbers to each receive offerings.
To be stingy with wealth and treasures is not considered a disgrace;
to be stingy with the sublime Dharma—that indeed is shameful.
This thing called stinginess inevitably brings a foul and disgraceful reputation;
one who removes parsimony and practices generosity is praised by the sages and saints.
O Benevolent One, if you persist in your resolve and do not grant me the relics;
Now you should immediately leave the city to compete in strength with your guest.
While staying within the city, rely on the door-panels; do not take up a staff to go forth and fight.
To do so would mean you are no king, neither noble nor a valiant hero.
The intentions of the kings outside the city are as previously described;
we both possess virtuous hearts, and thus the same principle is shown to both houses.
Furthermore, there is a private intention, desiring to direct it toward you, O Benevolent One.
I hope you will deign to listen for a moment; I pray that you will preach the True and Right Dharma.
O virtuous ones, do not be stubborn, nor focus your minds on seeking battle;
throughout the ages of war and strife, there has been neither righteous merit nor benefit.
The Buddha, the Teacher of Gods, has often sighed that the virtue of patience is foremost;
why now, O virtuous ones, do you burn with rage and seek battle?
Whether it be over the six desires, or over precious wealth and goods;
If one engages in such strife and contention, it may still be reconciled through reason and principle;
yet because of the power of merit, these wholesome dharmas are praised and extolled.
Since goodness is the enemy of contention, this meaning should be reflected upon with careful scrutiny.
Always with a mind of universal compassion, possessing a nature of harmony, tranquility, and peace;
following the teachings of the Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Men, one should bestow kindness upon all sentient beings.
Do not harm or kill sentient beings, but practice reverence and serve the Buddha.
In the end, there will be no benefit; this matter should not be so.
You, O virtuous ones, should open your minds and distribute the relics of the King;
the True Dharma shall thus be spread, and through this, it shall become beginningless.
If one can act in this way, there will be no further strife or contention;
one shall attain two kinds of excellence: merit and a good reputation.
Those who cling exclusively to their own views depart from the right path and enter onto a false one.
A virtuous person employs every means to lead others onto the right path.
When kings employ skillful means, desiring to widely establish the wholesome Dharma and universally guide the world,
they lead them to the realms of gods and humans.
The World-Honored One constantly praised and extolled that among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is the most excellent;
wherever he went, he was the teacher, and he was lauded by gods and humans alike.
Surveying all the worlds, he saw that those who give material wealth were not few.
"One who bestows the Dharma as a gift, whether at a time when it exists or does not exist,
gains a wide-reaching reputation for their Dharma-giving and brings vast peace and security to the world.
When this multitude of Mallas heard these words of the sublime Dharma;
Secretly harboring shame within his heart, he gazed intently at him in silence.
With words of humble affection and reverence, he spoke to the brahmin:
"Your Eminence possesses excellent skillful means; you bestow love and respect upon all."
To be a true brahmin is to be free from falsehood, diligently establishing oneself in what is wholesome.
One who can subdue themselves while treading the path of virtuous conduct is like a driver who restrains an unbroken horse, preventing it from entering among wild beasts.
We shall follow your intention, just as the Teacher has instructed;
with deep affection and sincere reverence, we shall listen to you.
Yet, you have suddenly abandoned those who speak words of loyalty and indignation—those upright ones who offer virtuous admonition.
"When the matter fails and one encounters hardship, subsequent regret will be of no avail.
Thereupon, with golden jars, he divided the relics of the Holy Honored One;
setting them apart into eight portions, he established them with singular equanimity.
Thereupon the Mallas took one portion from among them;
they set aside the remaining seven portions and sent them to the seven kings.
At that time, the Mallas hosted the visiting kings as honored guests.
The various kings, having obtained the relics, returned to their respective countries with a mixture of grief and joy.
Thereupon, the seven kings, each within their own realm,
raised armies to construct divine stupas, reaching as high as the limits of the clouds.
The brahmin, whose nature was like the fragrance of grass, desired to erect a stūpa for his own kin;
he then requested from the Mallas a measure of the jar containing the relics.
Being a noble brahmin within the boundaries, he further requested the ashes and charcoal where the Buddha had been cremated.
All together they gathered and collected [the relics], and with reverence erected divine stupas.
The various kings first initiated the construction of these stupas for the divine relics;
throughout the land of Jambudvīpa, their towering virtue was like a mountain.
The ninth is the Stūpa of the Golden Jar established by the Brahmin;
The Stūpa of the Buddha’s Accumulated Charcoal Ashes completes the ten, wondrous and majestic.
With flowers, incense, precious banners, and canopies, These manifest offerings to the Stūpas.
Adorned with exquisite beauty, like a mountain crag incensed with fragrance;
from neighboring kingdoms and towns, countless people gathered;
some wept with joy, while others paid homage and venerated the divine stūpa.
All together we pursue and long for you, remembering the Buddha’s meritorious virtues;
bitter, sorrowful, and agonizing, how extreme is your eternal departure!
You bestowed goodness upon the world, the very thing upon which all sentient beings rely.
A guide for those lost on the path, a skilled physician for the gravely ill;
a spring sun for the cold, a cool pond for those scorched by drought;
the canopy over the three realms has suddenly and utterly vanished into stillness.
The three realms have lost their protection; there is no one to rely upon—how pitiable!
They shall lose their way on the correct path, following what is false and encountering hardship.
The world has lost its rectitude and leans toward the perverse, flowing into the three evil destinies.
Who in this world possesses such great power that they could restrain him and cause him to return?
All sentient beings in the world have their eyes shrouded by ignorance;
they are being consumed by the fires of greed, lust, and hatred.
All sentient beings in the world are stricken with the grave illness of worldly afflictions;
the World-Honored One, with his heart of universal compassion, acts as the skilled physician for the three realms.
When the Buddha-sun, with its flourishing radiance, first appeared in the world;
A great radiance universally surges forth, Illuminating the three thousandfold world-system.
It causes the lotuses of gods and humans throughout the world To bloom everywhere;
Just as the flowers in various ponds Open when touched by the sun’s rays.
The devas, the people of the world, and the great kings,
weeping with sorrowful lamentation and longing, turned toward the stupa and chanted the Buddha’s virtues:
“O Great Protector of the World, supreme teacher of compassion;”
Suddenly you have abandoned all sentient beings; how can this be so exceedingly swift?
The radiance of the Buddha-sun has suddenly vanished;
with the mist of ignorance now shrouding the world, from where shall we behold the light again?
"Who shall guide sentient beings, showing them the path of the True Truths;
leading them to the city of Nirvāṇa, which is tranquil and free from fear?
At that time, the Mārṣa Guhyapada extensively [spoke] for the sake of all devas and humans:
He then expounded this Dharma in due order, proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha’s original practices.
When the devas heard what was said, their hair stood on end in awe;
reflecting upon the principles taught, they sought after the Buddha’s merits.
"The foundation of the manifold virtues accumulated is infinite and immeasurable;
it is the gathering of good deeds over incalculable kalpas.
By practicing the six perfections, one attains the ground that is as deep as the great ocean."
The wisdom of the marks of virtue from all jewels is full and overflowing.
Within this present Bhadrakalpa, there are a thousand bodhisattvas who have arisen;
even if all the arhats possessed wisdom like that of Śāriputra, [it would not equal theirs].
Even if one spent an entire kalpa extolling the Buddha’s virtues, one could never reach the end;
how much more so for me, whose wisdom is shallow and inferior, as I merely set forth what I have seen and heard.
At that time, the devas and humans gathered in the assembly heard the Dharma he preached.
Suddenly, within my heart, clear realization dawned; it was as if I were facing the Buddha in person.
All together we harbored a sense of sorrowful emotion, feeling deep compassion and longing for the Buddha.
We vowed to set our will upon the Mahāyāna, expressing our feelings with single-minded resolve.
I prostrate my head and take refuge in the Buddha; suddenly, each of them flew away.
